author: kha
body:
This PR extends the experimental module system with a phase distinction between `meta` and regular declarations. This distinction will be used in follow-up PRs to avoid importing IR that is not needed for compile-time execution.

The phase distinction system deliberately is the weakest one to implement this goal:
* `meta` declarations may use any local declaration, imported `meta` declarations, and any `meta import`ed declarations.
* non-`meta` declarations may use a non-`meta` declaration reachable only through non-`meta` imports.

Thus it is allowed and can be necessary to import the same module into both the `meta` and regular phase via two separate import statements. `meta import` is transitive in the sense that `import`ing a `meta import` is the same as writing the `meta import` inline.

Based on #8653

author: performance
body:
Implements a new service to analyze basic image quality metrics: brightness and contrast.

Key changes:
- Added `services/image_quality.py` with `analyze_image_quality` function. This function calculates:
    - Brightness: Mean pixel intensity of the grayscale image (0-1 scale).
    - Contrast: Standard deviation of pixel intensities in the grayscale image. It also provides textual insights like "image is dark", "image has low contrast", etc., based on predefined thresholds.
- Added new Pydantic models `ImageQualityMetrics` and `ImageQualityAnalysisResponse` in `main.py` for the API.
- Introduced a new API endpoint `/api/analysis/quality/{image_id}` in `main.py`. This endpoint retrieves an image by its ID, uses the `image_quality` service to perform the analysis, and returns the metrics and insights.
- Added comprehensive tests in `tests/test_image_quality.py` covering various scenarios (dark, bright, low/high contrast, balanced images) for both the service and the API endpoint. All tests pass and include checks for performance.

This addresses issue B007, enabling the system to analyze image quality for recommending auto-enhancements.

author: dhecht
body:
#### d6a6f29475b0e9a8ff0d85b0b73b1c18b6c922ff 
[libpas] Enumerator should not assume remote mappings persist across calls to memory_reader_t
https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=294130
rdar://143300973

Reviewed by Yusuke Suzuki.

A tool that calls into the enumerator provides a memory_reader_t
callback to allow the enumerator to map the remote memory of the
target process. The address returned by the memory_reader_t callback is
guaranteed to persist only to the next call to the memory_reader_t
callback. This is documented in malloc.h.

The libpas enumerator was violating this by keeping addresses alive
across calls to the reader callback.

A few techniques are used to fix this:

1. The libpas compact heap (which is limited in size and stores
   libpas metadata) is copied into the local process, and pointers
   into the remote compact heap are translated to local pointers using
   pointer arithmetic. The only change here is to copy the compact
   heap during pas_enumerator_create(). The accessors generated by
   the compact pointer macros do not change.

2. The libpas enumerator creates a hashtable containing references to
   the local allocators. The local allocators live within the TLCs and
   the baseline allocator table, so these regions are also copied into
   the local process. Then the local allocators are accessed directly
   via hashtable lookups, as before.

3. Some other important "root" structures are copied during
   pas_enumerator_create and referenced directly by the pas_enumerator
   structure (this was mostly already done in 277271@main).

4. The final piece of metadata needed before recording objects is the
   page header, which are variable sized. Rather than deal with copying
   these variable sized structures, a pinning interface is used to
   ensure no other mapping (i.e. calls to the reader callback) is
   established while using this pointer.

5. The lenient compact pointer case is a weird case where the pointer
   may reference either the compact heap or bounce through the compact heap
   to another heap. This is used to store the fully alloc bits, which
   sometimes come from the local allocator and sometimes from the
   compact heap and are variable sized data structure.
   These are copied out into a special purpose resizable buffer when
   necessary. This code can be deleted if the partial view code is deleted.

6. All other remote address accesses (the common case) are handled by
   copying the remote scalar or structure into an automatic stack variable.
   i.e. the enumerator doesn't get direct access to the mapped address
   and thus no pointer lifetime issues can exist. This requires reworking
   e.g. list and hashtable traversals a bit so that pointer dereferencing
   occurs up front rather than between iterations (because the
   current iteration will make another call into the reader callback,
   potentially invalidating the mapping holding the "next" pointer).

Testing:
- The IsoHeapChaosTests provides good coverage of the enumerator code,
  but the reader implementation was caching all previous mappings.
  Changed the test reader to clobber all previously returned buffers
  to emulate the behavior that pointers returned by the reader can be
  invalidated by the next reader call.
- Run leaks and heap tools on WebContent with these changes and see that
  they work.

author: belisarius222
body:
## 🤖 Installing Claude Code GitHub App

This PR adds a GitHub Actions workflow that enables Claude Code integration in our repository.

### What is Claude Code?

[Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code) is an AI coding agent that can help with:
- Bug fixes and improvements  
- Documentation updates
- Implementing new features
- Code reviews and suggestions
- Writing tests
- And more!

### How it works

Once this PR is merged, we'll be able to interact with Claude by mentioning @claude in a pull request or issue comment.
Once the workflow is triggered, Claude will analyze the comment and surrounding context, and execute on the request in a GitHub action.

### Important Notes

- **This workflow won't take effect until this PR is merged**
- **@claude mentions won't work until after the merge is complete**
- The workflow runs automatically whenever Claude is mentioned in PR or issue comments
- Claude gets access to the entire PR or issue context including files, diffs, and previous comments

### Security

- Our Anthropic API key is securely stored as a GitHub Actions secret
- Only users with write access to the repository can trigger the workflow
- All Claude runs are stored in the GitHub Actions run history
- Claude's default tools are limited to reading/writing files and interacting with our repo by creating comments, branches, and commits.
- We can add more allowed tools by adding them to the workflow file like:

```
allowed_tools: Bash(npm install),Bash(npm run build),Bash(npm run lint),Bash(npm run test)
```

There's more information in the [Claude Code documentation](http://docs.anthropic.com/s/claude-code-github-actions).

After merging this PR, let's try mentioning @claude in a comment on any PR to get started!

author: stnolting
body:
### Overview

Semihosting is a mechanism developed by ARM that enables code running on the NEORV32 to communicate and use the input/output facilities on a host computer that is running a debugger. Examples of these facilities include keyboard input, screen output, and disk I/O. For example, you can use this mechanism to enable functions in the C library, such as `printf()` and `scanf()`, to use the screen and keyboard of the host instead of having a screen and keyboard on the target system. (source: https://developer.arm.com/documentation/dui0471/i/semihosting/what-is-semihosting-?lang=en)

For example, with semihosting you can

* print to the host's `stdout` console
* read from the host's `stdin` console
* execute arbitrary command in the host's shell
* retrieve the host's system time
* read and write files on the host system
* ...

### Example Program

An example program is provided (`sw/example/demo_semihosting`) that showcases some of the semihosting features:

* read strings from the host's console - no UART required
* write string to the host's console - no UART required
* get the current system time from the host (this could be used to initialize the NEORV32 system timer)
* issue a command that gets executed on the host (`dir` is used as this is available on Windows and Linux - and this should cause no harm)
* read a file from the host system

### Further References

* A great overview: https://interrupt.memfault.com/blog/arm-semihosting
* Implementing semihosting on RISC-V: https://embeddedinn.com/articles/tutorial/understanding-riscv-semihosting/
* Description of the service calls by ARM: https://developer.arm.com/documentation/dui0203/j/semihosting/semihosting-operations?lang=en

body:
# Fix issue #829: Move freed page processing after transaction commit

## Problem
Issue #829 describes a race condition where freed pages from one transaction aren't immediately available for reuse in the next transaction. The problem occurs because `process_freed_pages()` is called before `mem.commit()` (which includes fsync), creating a window where pages could be reused before the freeing transaction is durably committed.

## Solution Approach
Following the suggestion in the issue comments, this PR moves `process_freed_pages()` to after `mem.commit()` in `WriteTransaction::durable_commit()`. This ensures that:

1. The transaction is durably committed first (via fsync)
2. Only then are freed pages processed and made available for allocation
3. A `non_durable_commit()` call updates the in-memory state to make freed pages immediately available

## Current Status - BLOCKED
The implementation is currently blocked by a page reference counting assertion:
```
Allocated a page that is still referenced! r0.1/0
```

The issue occurs because:
- `process_freed_pages()` tries to allocate pages for system tables to store freed page information
- These pages may be the same ones that were just freed but still have outstanding PageImpl references
- The debug assertion in `allocate_helper()` prevents allocation of pages that still have references

## Changes Made
- Modified `WriteTransaction::durable_commit()` to move `process_freed_pages()` after `mem.commit()`
- Added `non_durable_commit()` call to update in-memory state after processing freed pages
- Ensured proper mutex guard management to avoid borrow checker issues

## Test Case
The `page_reuse` test on the "reuse" branch demonstrates the expected behavior - freed pages should be immediately available for reuse in subsequent transactions.

## Next Steps
Need guidance on how to handle the page reference counting mechanism to allow reallocation of freed pages that may still have outstanding PageImpl references.

author: kilohertzian
body:
This commit addresses the missing error handling for the `mysofa_getfilter_float` function in `src/sofa/loader.rs`.

The following changes were made:
- The integer return code of `bindings::mysofa_getfilter_float` is now captured and checked against `MYSOFA_OK`.
- If an error is detected from the return code, the `err` field of the `MYSOFA_EASY` handle (`self.handle.err`) is also inspected to provide more detailed error information.
- A new error variant `SofaError::MysofaFilterError(String)` was added to propagate these errors.
- The `bindgen`-generated FFI bindings were found to be sufficient for this implementation, correctly providing the integer return type for `mysofa_getfilter_float` and access to the `err` field in `MYSOFA_EASY`.
- Added a unit test `test_get_hrtf_irs_error_handling` to verify the error propagation, though it cannot be run currently due to unrelated compilation issues in `src/lib.rs`.
- Updated `BUGS.md` to mark the corresponding issue as resolved.

author: fubuloubu
body:
### What I did

Add support for `pyproject.toml` for both plugin detection and extra packages

fixes: #35

### How I did it

`pyproject.toml` can serve 2 purposes:
1. define `[tool.ape]` config that supercedes `ape-config.yaml`
2. define extra packages in `[project.dependencies]` that supercedes `requirements.txt`

So we need to test 4 scenarios:
1. `requirements.txt` and `ape-config.yaml`
2. `pyproject.toml` (with no `[tool.ape]` config) and `ape-config.yaml`
3. `requirements.txt` and `pyproject.toml` (with `[tool.ape]` config but no `[project]` key)
4. `pyproject.toml` (with bot `[tool.ape]` config and `[project.dependencies]` keys)

### How to verify it

New tests
Also testing w/ https://github.com/fubuloubu/Purse/pull/7

author: zichengma
body:
This PR adds a component-level observability framework by embedding a lightweight HTTP server into each Dynamo service. It delivers:

- Unified HTTP Interface: Exposes both metrics and health probes over a single port per component, simplifying deployment and operations.

- Component-Level Metrics Migration: Currently @tedzhouhk implemented a [rust frontend metrics collection](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/1315). This PR may migrate the implementation. For other component, what metrics should be monitored still needs discussion.

- Health-Check Requirements: Defines appropriate probes and checks to support Kubernetes-style deployment patterns.

- Python & Rust Bindings: Provides APIs for registering custom health functions and configuring response thresholds programmatically.

author: mattash
body:
I refactored the test suite to improve consistency and organization. Here's what I completed:

I added missing `__init__.py` files to all test directories to ensure test discovery works properly. I converted all pytest-style tests to Django's unittest format, focusing on `test_aws_location.py`, `test_endpoints.py`, and `test_models.py`.

I created several key test infrastructure files:
- `tests/base.py` with base test classes providing common functionality
- `tests/fixtures/test_data.py` replacing pytest fixtures with a Django test factory
- `tests/test_settings.py` to handle Redis mocking and other test-specific settings

I organized tests into a clearer structure:
- `unit/` for model and utility tests
- `integration/` for API endpoint tests
- `functional/` for workflow tests
- `fixtures/` for test data utilities

I renamed `test_jwt.py` to `test_auth.py` for better clarity and removed pytest configuration files (`pytest.ini`, `conftest.py`). I also added comprehensive documentation in `tests/README.md` explaining test organization and execution.

The test suite now uses Django's unittest format consistently and all tests are properly discoverable. Tests can be run with `python manage.py test --settings=tests.test_settings`.

author: totten
body:
Overview ---------- This shuffles several of buildkit's built-in scripts into a different folder-structure, which will likely appear more familiar to PHP application-developers. Before+After ------------- |Aspect | Before | After |-- | -- | -- |Script Location | Single file in `src/pogo/XXX.php` | Folder in `tools/XXX/` |Dependency Declarations| Inline | `tools/XXX/composer.json` |Dependency Storage | `extern/XXX-php-VER` | `tools/XXX/vendor` |Stub References| `bin/XXX`
⇒ `src/pogo/XXX.php` | `bin/XXX`
⇒ `tools/XXX/run.php` |Setup Logic | Bash code in `civi-download-tools` | PHP script (`tools/install.php`) fired by top-level `composer install` For example: * __Before__: `bin/fetch-universe` <=> `src/pogo/fetch-universe.php` <=> `extern/fetch-universe-php-8.3/` * __After__: `bin/fetch-universe` <=> `tools/fetch-universe/` with files `run.php composer.json composer.lock vendor` Comments ---------- The general motivation is to trim `civi-download-tools` and make the subunits of `builkit.git` more discrete. Moving toward ^^ required _something_. It doesn't have to be this. (*I had an alternative approach that would continue using pogo -- and I almost went down that path.*) But my guess is that other folks (cc @demeritcowboy @seamuslee001) will be happier with this layout. Other comments: * In ancient times, these scripts all used one shared `composer.json` for dependencies. Updates were painful -- someone would bump up package X for tool A, validate tool A, and then break tool B. In their essence, these scripts are independent entities -- IMHO, there's no world where it makes sense for `fetch-universe` and `civicredits` and `zipdiff` to share the same dependency metadata. (But at the same time, they're not quite big enough to justify the overhead of managing independent projects.) * I've actually been fairly happy with the `pogo` arrangement from a runtime POV and dependency-management POV. (It solved some gnarly dependency-resolution issues around php72 vs php83.) OTOH, it *is* annoying to edit the scripts in an IDE (or to use breakpoints), and it is out-of-mainstream. Some of the scripts would be nicer if split into smaller PHP files. There are silver-linings to a more traditional layout. * In this moment (following the expulsion of php71+php72), the scripts all get similar dependency-resolutions across the spread (php74...php84).

## Describe your changes

- Upgrades all markdown-related dependencies (react-markdown, unified, rehype, remark) and makes code changes to support our usecases given the deprecations and changes that have happened in these major versions.
- One of the main benefits is that this should be a lot faster from a performance perspective. There are some updates in the underlying libraries that make parsing faster!

Using the code from #11550:
Before:
![Screenshot 2025-06-09 at 4 04 26 PM](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/1e2814c6-44e9-4a7d-9528-5c83d736cf82)

After:
![Screenshot 2025-06-09 at 4 03 38 PM](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/61cdec0b-965d-48fd-b00a-43c8333f5fd6)

4.5 seconds -> 50ms = **98% decrease**.

Note that these screenshots are from dev mode with React StrictMode on, so this is being rendered twice without optimizations. Real world timings on prod builds will be shorter for both scenarios.

## GitHub Issue Link (if applicable)

Fixes #11550

- Explanation of why no additional tests are needed
- Unit Tests (JS and/or Python)
- E2E Tests
- Any manual testing needed?

author: atxtechbro
body:
## Description

This PR fixes the shellcheck warning that's causing the CI lint job to fail in PR #385.

## Changes

- Added a shellcheck directive `# shellcheck disable=SC1090` before sourcing ~/.bash_aliases
- This tells shellcheck to ignore the SC1090 warning for non-constant source paths

## Issue Fixed

The CI job was failing with the following warning:
```
In setup.sh line 573:
  source ~/.bash_aliases
         ^-------------^ SC1090 (warning): ShellCheck can't follow non-constant source. Use a directive to specify location.
```

This is a common shellcheck warning that occurs when sourcing files with paths that can't be statically analyzed. Since ~/.bash_aliases is a valid path that we've already checked exists with the if statement, it's safe to disable this specific warning.

## Testing

- Verified locally that shellcheck no longer reports this warning when run with the directive in place
